evidence_set: Face task: Ekman faces of four emotions (anger, fear, happiness, sadness) morphed from neutral to full expression in 10% steps, plus 10 neutral faces (170 pictures), each shown for 500 ms and answered by choosing one of the four emotions or neutral; accuracy as proportion correct. Eyes test of 36 eye regions showing complex emotions; DANVA-2, 24 recorded voice clips. Drug by emotion interaction for faces F(5.2,104.6) = 3.23, p = 0.008; fear F(2.8,56.0) = 4.45, p = 0.008, eta squared 0.18. Proportion of fearful faces correctly named, mean (SD): placebo 0.63 (0.07), MDMA 0.75 mg/kg 0.59 (0.12), MDMA 1.5 mg/kg 0.55 (0.10), methamphetamine 0.59 (0.10); placebo against MDMA 1.5 mg/kg t(20) = 3.94, significant after Bonferroni correction; placebo against MDMA 0.75 mg/kg t(20) = 2.27, against methamphetamine 2.59, MDMA 0.75 against 1.5 mg/kg 1.41 and MDMA 1.5 mg/kg against methamphetamine 1.31, none significant after Bonferroni correction (placebo against MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and against methamphetamine would be p of about 0.03 and 0.02 uncorrected, editors' calculation). Happy 0.74, 0.71, 0.71, 0.73 (F(3,60) = 0.96); sad 0.51, 0.54, 0.47, 0.52 (3.60); angry 0.64, 0.63, 0.59, 0.63 (2.0); neutral 0.69, 0.68, 0.77, 0.67 (2.84): not significant after correction. Eyes test total 26.81, 26.67, 26.10, 27.24 (F(3,60) = 0.58) and voices (n = 20) 18.05, 18.00, 17.20, 18.70 (F(3,57) = 3.01), both reported as not affected by MDMA. Exploratory: number of emotional faces misclassified as neutral 44.90 (SD 11.31) after placebo against 51.71 (10.58) after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (t(20) = 2.52, p < 0.05 uncorrected). Editors' calculations: fear, a fall of 0.08 (about 0.04 to 0.12 from the printed t and the rounded means), within-person standardized difference about 0.86 (3.94 divided by the square root of 21); the voice F(3,57) = 3.01 corresponds to p of about 0.04 before any sphericity correction, which the paper does not print.

The authors call identifying others' emotions an important first step in empathy, and describe their earlier imaging study (Bedi et al., 2009) as finding no change in the accuracy of identifying emotions in faces, whose expressions were not subtle and were shown for 4 seconds. They suggest the new pattern may be more consistent with increased social approach than with increased empathy: MDMA may ease social interaction by reducing the impact of others' negative emotions rather than by improving recognition of them. Limits they name: static photographs may be less true to life than moving faces; no task compared social with non-social pictures; the methamphetamine dose was not adjusted for body weight; all participants had used ecstasy before, so the findings may not apply to people new to MDMA.

Targeted check 2026-11-14 (AI reader 688 (round-2 check)): not found at the stated place. no PDF on file. Bedi 2010 (PDF p. 2) confirms only that the 2009 study found no change in emotion-identification accuracy, with 4-second displays; none of the 2009 numbers can be checked here.

evidence_set: 10 men and 10 women had sometimes taken cannabis with MDMA and said the main effect of adding it was more desire; the ratings were said to refer to MDMA alone, and the authors report no difference in any rating between those who did and did not add cannabis, without data. The Discussion calls the effects on erection inconsistent, while the Summary reports erection impaired in 40% of the men without the 40% who reported better erections, and the conclusion says MDMA seems to impair sexual performance in spite of more desire and the perception of greater satisfaction. Limits named by the authors: a sample not randomly selected, of people willing to describe use of an illegal drug; retrospective recall open to inaccuracy; unknown dose and purity of the pills; cannabis use by about half; and expected effects of the drug (a placebo effect), which should not be disregarded.

Qualitative study reported by a single author: face-to-face, semi-structured, in-depth interviews of 1 to 2 hours, taped and transcribed, conducted by four trained interviewers (two of them the project directors) with current and former ecstasy users in Northern Ireland, October 1997 to November 1998; 106 interviewed and 8 discarded for recording or transcription problems, leaving 98. Recruited through notices in shops and health centres, a club and music magazine, local agencies (including sexually transmitted disease clinics and gay and lesbian outreach), the interviewers' own contacts, referral by respondents and paid recruiters (10 pounds per referral and completed interview); clubs were not used. 69% men; aged 17 to 45 (mean 25); 16% gay or bisexual; 92% had used ecstasy in the past 6 months and 44% on at least 100 occasions. Effects attributed to MDMA refer to what respondents believed they had taken, as tablet content varies. The article describes no method of analysis and counts no finding.
Methods, 1st to 3rd and 5th paragraphs and footnote c (pp. 1463-1464); Description of Respondents, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 1464-1465); Table 1 (p. 1465); Table 2 (p. 1466)

Several respondents who had sex during ecstasy episodes, more often those aged about 18 to 25, described behaviours carrying a risk of infection: multiple partners and one-night stands with strangers or distant acquaintances; a number voiced regret the next day. Condom use was rare during ecstasy episodes that involved intercourse, but few respondents reported using condoms when no drugs had been taken either. Asked whether ecstasy or alcohol brought more sexual risk, respondents gave mixed views; because a number of respondents took alcohol and other substances in the same episodes, the author says their effects are hard to disentangle.

Interactions of MDMA with alcohol and cannabis could not be examined, and the author says prospective data might be needed, with detailed timing of drug use and sex, as recall of heavy multi-drug episodes may be affected. The abstract states findings more strongly than the text: most respondents (the text: a slight majority) reported closeness without wanting penetrative sex; gay and bisexual women in particular had used MDMA for sexual enhancement, which the Discussion says their small number in the sample does not allow to be concluded; and sexual risk taking was prevalent among those who had sex during MDMA episodes, without counts and without the finding that condoms were also rare without drugs. The data are from 1997 and 1998; the author says the scene has probably changed and that it is unclear whether the findings apply now.

evidence_set: Vasopressin peaked between 1 and 2 hours after the dose: baseline range 1.14 to 1.88 pmol/L, 2-hour range 2.46 to 9.16 pmol/L (paired t test, p = 0.006, one-tailed; about 0.012 two-tailed, editors' calculation); the geometric mean concentrations in the figure contrast with a small decrease on the 3 control occasions, which appear only as a line in the figure and are not compared statistically with the MDMA occasions. Vasopressin and MDMA concentrations were not correlated (Spearman r = 0.2, p = 0.1), which the authors say is probably because of vasopressin's rapid clearance (initial half-life about 6 minutes).

The authors call the dose relatively small (stating, without a source, that street ecstasy frequently contains more than 100 mg), say the rise came at a time of day when vasopressin would not be expected to change, and conclude that the low-sodium illness is likely linked to MDMA's ability to stimulate vasopressin secretion, that with excessive fluid even a small dose could lead to symptoms, and that the rise does not seem to be part of a general stress response because cortisol did not change significantly. The letter tested neither of the first two conclusions: it gave no fluid load, measured no urine and studied no illness; the third rests on a non-significant cortisol rise in 8 men; and its closing message about fluid intake and its statement on thirst and judgement rest on no data from the study.

In 32 healthy volunteers (16 women) given MDMA 125 mg or placebo, double blind, in a crossover design (random order stated in the abstract), plasma copeptin, which the paper names C-terminal provasopressin, was measured before and 1 and 2 hours after the capsule; MDMA did not alter it (no statistic printed), while oxytocin, cortisol and prolactin rose. Figure 4B shows mean peak changes of about +1.7 pg/mL after MDMA and about -1.1 pg/mL after placebo in all participants, with no significance mark (editors' reading). Sodium was not measured.
